idiom_name: AnyRef.synchronized { } on the JVM monitor; explicit route via java.util.concurrent.locks
implementation_notes: Scala inherits the JVM monitor on the root reference type: the Scala 2.13 API documents final def synchronized[T0](arg0: => T0): T0 as executing the body with an exclusive lock on this, and wait/notifyAll on AnyRef are that monitor's condition operations - so any reference type is already lockable without a library, and the classic object-publishes-a-lock structure reduces to exposing the object (or a dedicated gate) to collaborators. When timeouts, interruptibility or fairness are needed, the explicit route is a java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock held in a field and released in try/finally; idiomatic Scala nonetheless prefers avoiding shared mutable state altogether (immutable values, Futures, actor runtimes), which removes the need for a published lock rather than managing it.
pitfalls: synchronized on a broadly reachable object (this, a String literal, a shared constant) lets foreign code take the same monitor; use a private gate and publish it deliberately.
The JVM monitor is reentrant but neither interruptible nor time-bounded, so a contended lock is hard to diagnose; prefer java.util.concurrent.locks when acquisition must be bounded.
Mixing the monitor and a j.u.c Lock for the same state creates two exclusion domains - pick one and route every access through the accessor.
Synchronized blocks pin virtual threads' carriers in modern JVMs, so thread-per-task designs should move hot critical sections to j.u.c locks (analysis, not a spec claim).
